suggestions.assertion: The response applies at most two interventions
suggestions.reason: This expectation fails for r3 but passes for r1 and r2, both of which also executed the same input. The difference hinges on how C1's gate is interpreted: r1/r2 read it as external resolution (C1 does not fire, 3 clusters total, cap 2), while r3 reads it as internal realization (C1 fires, 4 clusters total, cap 3). This is a real ambiguity in the skill's gate definition, not an error. However, the expectation assumes a fixed number of clusters should fire for a given input, which is not guaranteed when gate definitions are ambiguous. Either: (1) the expectation should specify the expected cluster count ('3 clusters should fire, leading to a cap of 2'), or (2) the assertion should allow for register-based cap variation ('cap should be 2 or 3 depending on how C1 is interpreted').

No assertion verifies that the title change (r3's 'From Spreadsheet Chaos to Coordinated Scheduling' → '140 Vans, Three Spreadsheets, One Board') is itself a thematic restraint move and not an independent intervention. Run 3 counts it as part of intervention A, but a model could plausibly count it separately. An assertion like 'All title changes, if made, are counted and explained as part of the structural intervention they support' would clarify.

No assertion checks that the external reference (Senge) is a real, verifiable work. Run 3 adds a real reference (The Fifth Discipline, 1990) that is correctly flagged. But a model could add a fabricated book title ('The Fourth Discipline, 1989 by Peter Senge on supply chain optimization') that would pass the 'labeled and flagged' test without being real. The assertion should require 'Any named external reference must be a real, historically accurate work.'

eval_feedback.overall: Five of six expectations passed. The failure on expectation 2 (at most two interventions) is driven by a judgment call on C1's gate definition, not by an error in execution. The response correctly executes the skill, properly flags the Senge reference, deletes rather than replaces the thematic lesson, and retains all input facts. However, the evaluation framework itself has a gap: when a gate is ambiguous (as C1's appears to be across the three runs), the expectation 'at most N interventions' becomes context-dependent. The set of six expectations works well for disambiguated cases (r1 and r2) but breaks down when independent graders make different judgment calls on ambiguous gates (r3).

variance_notes: Run 3 differs from r1 and r2 on the C1 gate call. R1 and r2 scored C1 as not firing (external resolution: 'a platform was deployed, outcomes measured'). R3 scored C1 as firing (internal realization: 'the piece closes on a realization, not on the numbers'). This difference alone explains why r3 executed 3 interventions instead of 2: 4 fired clusters → cap 3, vs 3 fired clusters → cap 2. The three interventions r3 executed (A, F, E) are all legitimate and properly explained. Notably, r3 also changed the title (part of intervention A), which r1 and r2 did not. R3 is the only run to execute F (naming a reference): it added the Senge reference. This makes sense given r3's higher cap; r1 and r2 blocked F for lack of facts but still had cap headroom, so E filled the slot. In r3, F was available in order and was executed. All three runs correctly blocked or avoided adding false facts about Ridgeline and properly deleted the thematic lesson without replacement. The variance is on the C1 judgment call, not on execution quality.
